readerTitle: Four decisions that decide your salary
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (호텔 레스토랑 주방 관리자가 가사 청소 서비스 회사의 운영 관리자 자리를 두고 연봉 협상) · 모든 인물과 수치는 설명용
insight: 연봉 협상의 승부는 대화 중의 말솜씨보다 대화 전에 정한 대안과 하한선, 그리고 상대가 내건 숫자 뒤의 이유를 묻는 데서 갈린다.
misconception: 연봉 협상은 기본급 숫자 하나를 두고 누가 더 버티느냐의 싸움이다. 처음 부른 숫자는 끝까지 지켜야 한다.

sources.text: Fisher, R. & Ury, W. (1981). Getting to Yes. BATNA 개념의 출처
Galinsky, A. & Mussweiler, T. (2001). First offers as anchors. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. 첫 제안의 앵커링 효과
인물, 회사, 급여 수치는 모두 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 급여 수치는 설명용 가상 수치이며 특정 지역이나 직종의 실제 시세가 아닙니다. 계산 확인: 대안(잔류) $55,000 + 주중 근무의 가치 약 $3,000 = 하한선 $58,000. 최종 기본급 $60,000 − 하한선 $58,000 = $2,000. 6개월 후 조건 충족 시 $65,000.
첫 제안의 앵커링 효과는 Galinsky & Mussweiler(2001) 등 협상 연구에서 반복 확인된 내용입니다. 카드에는 구체적 효과 크기를 적지 않았습니다. 인용 서지 정보를 게시 전에 다시 확인하세요.
연봉 협상 관행은 나라, 업종, 노조·공공부문 급여 체계에 따라 크게 다릅니다. Watch out 카드에 이 한계를 적었고, 특정 국가의 노동법 조언은 담지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Four decisions that decide your salary
body: Dana runs the kitchen at a busy hotel restaurant. A growing home-cleaning company wants her as its operations manager: scheduling crews, handling complaints, keeping bookings full.
The interview went well. Now comes the part most people dread: talking about money. You'll make four calls for her, one after another.

image.label: A kitchen manager in an apron looking at a job offer letter
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 앞치마를 두른 주방 관리자가 주방 뒤편에서 휴대폰 속 채용 제안 화면을 보고 있음. 한쪽에는 냄비와 주문표, 다른 쪽 창밖으로 청소 도구를 실은 작은 밴. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What Dana knows before the call
body: Before the call, Dana writes down the facts.
list: **If she stays:** the hotel has offered $55,000
**The market:** similar operations jobs in her city are posted at $58,000–$68,000
**The new job:** weekdays only, which matters to her family
cards.callout: The cleaning company knows none of this yet.

cards.title: What should Dana settle before the call?

options.text: The number she'd love to get, so she can aim high
options.feedback: A good target, but a dream number doesn't tell her when to say no. Without a floor, anything close to it will feel acceptable.

options.text: Nothing yet. Hear their offer first, then react
options.feedback: She stays flexible but gives up control. Any offer will sound fine in the moment, even one below what staying would pay.

options.text: Her best option if this falls through, and the lowest package she'd accept
options.feedback: Her fallback is staying at $55,000 with weekends. Weekdays off are worth about $3,000 a year to her, so her floor is $58,000. Now she knows when to walk.

cards.title: Say you chose C. The owner asks: "What are you expecting?"

options.text: "$68,000, based on posted roles and my experience running a team of twelve."
options.feedback: A specific first number with a reason pulls the talk toward it. The owner may counter, but from near $68,000, not $55,000.
Polite, but it hands the owner the first number. If they say $54,000, Dana starts below her own floor.
It sounds flexible, but the owner will hear $58,000. Dana has just opened with her floor.

cards.title: Say you chose A. The owner replies: "Our cap for this role is $60,000."
body: That's above Dana's floor, but well below her ask.

options.feedback: A safe deal, but she stops at the owner's position without learning why it's there. Value may be left on the table.

options.text: Hold firm at $68,000 or walk away
options.feedback: She protects her number but may lose a job she wants over a figure the owner truly can't move this year.

options.text: Ask what's behind the cap, then look at other terms
options.feedback: The owner explains: the other managers earn $60,000, and cash is tight before the spring rush. That opens room for a raise tied to results, or extra time off.

cards.title: Say you chose C. Here's the new offer.
body: **$60,000** to start. A written review at six months, rising to $65,000 if she cuts missed bookings to an agreed target. Five extra paid days off. The owner needs an answer by Friday.

options.text: Accept. It clears her floor and beats staying
options.feedback: The base alone is $2,000 above her floor, before the review and the days off. She gets a good deal and starts with goodwill.

options.text: Keep pushing for $68,000. That was her number
options.feedback: Her first number was an anchor, not a limit. Pushing past a deal that already works can cost the trust she'll need on day one.

options.text: Mention the hotel's counteroffer to squeeze out a little more
options.feedback: It might add a bit, but the hotel offered less than this. If the owner asks for the figure, the leverage is gone.

cards.title: The deal had to fit between two limits.

breakdown.label: Dana's floor
breakdown.detail: Alternative plus the value of weekdays off

breakdown.label: Agreed base
breakdown.detail: The owner's real cap this year

breakdown.label: After six months
breakdown.detail: If missed bookings hit the target

breakdown.label: Dana's opening ask
breakdown.detail: The anchor that set the range

cards.softwareNote: In software jobs the extra terms often include equity, a signing bonus or remote days. Same move: when the base is capped, ask why, then trade on what costs the company less than it's worth to you.

cards.title: These moves have limits.
body: An ambitious first number needs a real reason behind it. A number pulled from the air can make you look unprepared or unrealistic.
You'll work with this person every day. Bluffing about other offers or squeezing every dollar can win the call and cost the relationship.
And some employers can't negotiate at all: fixed pay scales, union contracts or public-sector bands. There, the extra terms may be the only room you have.

cards.title: Know your floor, name a number, then ask why.
body: Each of Dana's decisions used one idea from this unit.
list: **Before the call:** your best alternative sets your walk-away point
**First number:** a reasoned anchor shapes the whole range
**"Our cap is $60,000":** ask about interests behind the position, then expand the pie
**The final offer:** say yes when it sits inside the zone where both sides gain
cards.callout: **Try it today:** write down your best alternative to a deal you're working on, and the lowest terms you'd accept. Then list two things besides price you could trade.
